scenes.narration: [serious] A spy program hid inside the company that catches spy programs.
In 2011, experts in Hungary found a spy program. They named it Duqu. It looked like a famous virus that broke Iran's machines.
Then Duqu went quiet for years.
In 2015, the security company Kaspersky checked its own computers. Its own test tool found strangers inside.
Duqu was back. It hid only in the computer's memory, so it was hard to find.
The same spies also attacked hotels hosting Iran's nuclear talks.
No country has been officially blamed. The hunters had become the hunted.

facts.claim: Symantec was alerted to Duqu by the CrySyS lab at Budapest University of Technology and Economics on October 14, 2011; it was nearly identical to Stuxnet but built for espionage, and named for files with the prefix ~DQ
Duqu went dark in 2012; Duqu 2.0 ran only in memory and disappeared on reboot

Kaspersky detected the intrusion in early spring 2015 with a prototype anti-APT tool, announced it June 10, 2015, linked it to the 2011 Duqu group, said up to three zero-days were used, and called it a likely nation-state operation
Some 2014-2015 infections were linked to venues of the P5+1 Iran nuclear talks
Duqu 2.0 used a digital certificate stolen from Foxconn
Kaspersky did not name a country; media reports citing former U.S. officials pointed at Israel, which is not an official attribution

seo.title: Duqu 2.0: The Spy Malware That Hacked Kaspersky and the Iran Talks
seo.description: Duqu, a spying cousin of Stuxnet, was found in 2011 and then went quiet. In 2015 it came back inside Kaspersky's own network and at hotels hosting the Iran nuclear talks. Learn what Duqu 2.0 malware was and how Kaspersky found it. #cybersecurity #duqu #cyberespionage #shorts
